blocks.text: Handle many I/O sources on few threads: wait for readiness, then dispatch each ready event to its handler.

A **demultiplexer** blocks until some sources are ready and returns them. The **reactor** loop then calls the handler registered for each event, on a single thread. Handlers must be short and non-blocking, because they run on the loop itself.

items: **Inverts control:** you register interest; the loop calls you.
**Scales:** thousands of idle connections cost memory, not threads.
**Contract:** a handler that blocks stalls every other source.

blocks.text: This is the model behind `java.nio.channels.Selector`, Netty and Node.js: one loop, many channels.

walkthrough.note: The vocabulary: an operation kind, a ready event naming its channel, and a demultiplexer whose `select` returns the next batch of ready events.
The loop selects, then dispatches each event to the handler registered for its operation. An empty batch ends the loop. No other threads exist.
A lambda replays scripted batches, standing in for the OS; a real one blocks in `Selector.select()`. Handlers share `open` without locks: only the loop thread runs them.

blocks.text: A chat gateway holding 100,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections.

Almost every connection is silent at any moment. A thread per connection would burn memory on blocked stacks. The gateway runs a few event loops, each owning a share of the sockets. A loop wakes when bytes arrive, decodes the frame, and calls the pipeline; slow work, such as a database lookup, is handed to a separate executor.
Payoff: four threads serve 100,000 connections, and each connection's handlers run on one loop without locks.

lists.title: Use when
items: Many connections are mostly idle and work per event is small.
You want few threads and handlers that need no locks.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Each event needs long computation or blocking calls on the loop thread.
Concurrency is modest and a thread (or virtual thread) per connection reads simply.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Blocking in a handler stalls every channel on that loop.
Callback chains scatter one logical flow across handlers and make errors hard to trace.
A busy loop with unbounded work per event starves other channels.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Virtual threads make blocking thread-per-connection cheap enough for many workloads that once required a reactor.
Reactors remain the base of Netty and most async servers, but you rarely hand-roll one.

rows.difference: Observer notifies subscribers of state changes in-process. A reactor waits on I/O readiness from the OS and dispatches by event type, usually to one handler.
Producer-consumer passes work between threads through a queue. A reactor has no hand-off: the same thread detects the event and runs its handler.
Handlers that must block are offloaded to a pool so the loop stays responsive. Netty and Tomcat's NIO connector use this split.
An active object serializes requests to one object on its own thread. A reactor serializes I/O events for many channels on one loop.
Netty's channel pipeline is a chain of handlers that each event passes through after the loop has dispatched it.

entries.name: java.nio.channels.Selector
entries.detail: `select()` blocks until registered channels are ready, then `selectedKeys()` yields them for dispatch.

entries.name: EventLoop / NioEventLoopGroup
entries.detail: Each channel is bound to one event loop thread, and its pipeline handlers run there.

entries.name: libuv event loop
entries.detail: A single-threaded loop dispatches I/O callbacks via epoll, kqueue or IOCP.

entries.name: Vertx event loop
entries.detail: Verticles run on event loop threads and must not block them.

options.why: One thread waits for readiness on many channels and dispatches each ready one to its handler.
Observers are called when a subject changes. Here a blocking wait on the OS decides what is ready.
There is no queue between threads: the same thread detects the event and handles it.
No worker threads or task queue appear; everything runs on the loop thread.

exercises.scenario: A metrics collector accepts 20,000 long-lived TCP connections. Each sends a tiny packet every 30 seconds. The team wants a handful of threads and per-packet work takes a few microseconds.

options.why: A few loops wait on readiness for all sockets and dispatch tiny handlers, so idle connections cost no threads.
A thread per connection would be blocked on reads almost all the time, wasting thousands of threads.
The work is not recursive CPU-bound splitting; it is many sources waiting for I/O.
One queue and thread per connection would reintroduce thousands of threads and add futures nobody needs.

exercises.prompt: Explain the Reactor pattern in your own words: who waits, who runs the handlers, and what must a handler never do?

modelAnswer.text: A reactor thread blocks in a demultiplexer, such as `Selector.select`, until some channels are ready. It then calls the handler registered for each ready event, on that same thread. A few threads can serve thousands of connections. Handlers must never block or run long, since that stalls every other channel.

keyPoints: One loop waits for readiness on many sources
The same thread dispatches to registered handlers
Handlers run on the loop and must not block
Offload slow work to an executor
Virtual threads reduce, but do not remove, the need for it
